why_this_tool: Kubeflow makes the distributed training job a declarative Kubernetes resource, so the platform work of this lesson (launching the worker group, wiring it together, recovering it) is something you can inspect and automate on a local cluster.
alternatives: Ray Train with KubeRay scales a training loop from Python on a Ray cluster instead of declaring a Kubernetes resource, a raw JobSet or MPI launcher gives the worker group with no training runtime on top, and PyTorch Lightning or Hugging Face Transformers handle the in-process distribution strategy but leave launching and recovery to the platform.

setup.do: Read the installation methods and choose a standalone install of the Trainer and Pipelines components on a local kind or minikube cluster, with no cloud account and no GPU.
setup.done_when: You have written down which install method and which subprojects you will put on the local cluster.
setup.why: Kubeflow is a set of subprojects, and a laptop cannot comfortably hold the full distribution. Picking only the pieces this lesson needs keeps the cluster small enough to run.

setup.do: Install the Kubeflow Trainer control plane on the local cluster by following the Trainer documentation entry page.
setup.done_when: The Trainer controller pod reports Running in the local cluster.
setup.why: The Trainer controller is what turns a training job resource into a group of worker pods. Nothing in the later steps runs without it.

setup.do: Install the Kubeflow Pipelines SDK in a fresh Python virtual environment and point it at the local cluster.
setup.done_when: Importing the SDK in Python succeeds and it can reach the local Pipelines endpoint.
setup.why: The path drives training jobs from pipeline steps, so the SDK and its connection to the cluster have to work first.

steps.do: Run a first Python function-based component that only prints its inputs, inside a one-step pipeline on the local cluster.
steps.done_when: The run shows as succeeded and the pod log contains the printed inputs.

verified.section_found: Getting started with Python function-based components

steps.why: This proves the whole chain from laptop to cluster pod before any training code is involved. Later failures are then about training, not plumbing.

steps.do: Read what Kubeflow Trainer is and note which parts belong to the training framework and which to the platform.
steps.done_when: You can list, from memory, what the Trainer does for a job and what it leaves to PyTorch.
steps.why: In data-parallel training the framework synchronises gradients while the platform launches the workers and connects them. Knowing the split tells you where to look when a job hangs.

steps.do: Write a small PyTorch DistributedDataParallel training function for two CPU workers, using the Trainer introduction to see how workers receive their rank and peers; CPU workers stand in for GPU nodes here.
steps.done_when: The function runs locally in two processes and both print the same loss after each step.
steps.why: Data-parallel training means every worker holds a model copy, trains on its own shard and averages gradients each step. Writing it for two CPU workers shows the mechanism without a GPU.

steps.do: Create a training job as a Kubernetes resource from a pipeline step, using the resource operation to submit a two-worker job manifest for your function.
steps.done_when: Listing the training job resource shows it created, and two worker pods start together and finish.

source.title: Manipulate Kubernetes Resources as Part of a Pipeline | Kubeflow

steps.why: This is the core object model of Kubeflow Trainer: a distributed job is a declared resource the controller reconciles. Submitting it from a pipeline makes it one repeatable step.

steps.do: Create a persistent volume claim from the pipeline and mount it into the workers as the checkpoint directory.
steps.done_when: After a run, checkpoint files are visible on the volume from a separate pod.

source.title: Manipulate Kubernetes Resources as Part of a Pipeline | Kubeflow

steps.why: Worker pods are disposable, so a checkpoint written to pod storage dies with the pod. A shared volume is what makes recovery possible at all.

steps.do: Run the job again with the volume attached, delete one worker pod mid-training, and confirm the restarted job resumes from the last checkpoint.
steps.done_when: The log of the restarted worker reports loading a checkpoint and continues from a later step than zero.

source.title: Manipulate Kubernetes Resources as Part of a Pipeline | Kubeflow

steps.why: Fault tolerance is only real once you have watched a failure and a resume. One lost worker stalls the whole group, so the restart behaviour matters more than in single-node training.

steps.do: Create a volume snapshot of the checkpoint volume after two runs with different worker counts, and compare the saved metrics of both.
steps.done_when: Two snapshots exist and you have a side-by-side note of final loss and wall time for both runs.

source.title: Manipulate Kubernetes Resources as Part of a Pipeline | Kubeflow

steps.why: Snapshots keep each run's state so you can compare results instead of overwriting them. Comparing one worker against two shows what scaling out really bought you.

steps.do: Package a Ray Train version of the same training loop as a lightweight component, declaring ray in its packages to install, and run it with two local CPU workers.
steps.done_when: The component run succeeds and its log shows two Ray Train workers reporting metrics.
steps.why: Ray Train scales the loop from inside Python rather than through a job resource. Running both styles side by side makes the trade-off concrete.

steps.do: Configure a fixed base image for the training components instead of installing packages at start-up.
steps.done_when: The worker pods show your pinned image tag and start without a package install phase in the log.

verified.section_found: Selecting or building a container image

steps.why: All workers must run identical framework versions or they fail to synchronise. A pinned image also removes install time from every worker start.

steps.do: Compare the two approaches against the reasons the Trainer overview gives for using it, and record which one you would give to which team.
steps.done_when: You have a short written comparison covering launch model, failure recovery and who owns the job definition.
steps.why: A platform engineer has to recommend one path per use case. The overview gives the criteria the Trainer was designed around.

steps.do: Configure the Kubernetes platform-specific settings of the pipeline, such as resource requests, volumes and node selection, in the pipeline definition itself; where a GPU request is expected, use a CPU request locally.
steps.done_when: A fresh run from the definition alone produces worker pods with the requests and mounts you declared.
steps.why: Settings applied by hand on the cluster are lost on the next run. Keeping them in the pipeline definition makes the job reproducible by anyone and by CI.

steps.do: Compile the pipeline to a pinned definition file, commit it, and reproduce the full run from that file on a clean local cluster.
steps.done_when: The run launched from the committed file on a fresh cluster finishes with the same worker count and a checkpoint on the volume.
steps.why: The compiled file is the artifact an automated job can submit without your laptop environment. Reproducing it on a clean cluster is the closest laptop test of how it will behave elsewhere.
